title: Crime & deviance
examples: How reliable are official crime statistics really?
What is the difference between crime and deviance?
Do statistics tell the whole story about crime?

explain.say: Today we will look at how we measure crime in society.
One source is the police recorded crime statistics.
Another source is victim surveys, which ask people directly.
We can also look at official court records for prosecutions.
In real life, think about vandalism in your local area.
A common mistake is assuming police stats show everything.

faq.a: No, they only record what the police are aware of or what is reported to them. People might not report everything they experience.

faq.q: How does a victim survey help us?
faq.a: Victim surveys give us insight into crimes that never reached the police force. They capture the experience of the victim.
asks: What is the benefit of victim surveys?

faq.q: What is the difference between crime and deviance?
faq.a: Deviance is simply behaviour that breaks a social norm, while crime is behaviour that breaks a specific law. Not all deviance is illegal.
asks: What is the link between deviance and law?

faq.q: Can we use statistics to prove anything about crime?
faq.a: Statistics can show trends and patterns, but they cannot prove individual guilt or explain the complex reasons behind criminal behaviour.
asks: What can statistics really tell us?

faq.q: Do different sources count the same crime differently?
faq.a: Yes, for example, a minor dispute might be recorded as a police incident but never lead to a formal court charge.
asks: Are police and courts always in agreement?

facts: Official crime statistics are based on recorded incidents.
Victim surveys aim to capture unreported crime experiences.
Deviance refers to behaviour that breaks social rules, not just laws.
Police records show what the police are aware of.

quiz.say: If a student skips class because they feel unwell, this is best described as:
quiz.why: Skipping class breaks the school's rule, which is a social norm, making it deviance, even if it is not against the law.

wrong.1: Crime requires breaking a specific written law, which skipping class does not do.
wrong.2: A statistic is a number or data point, not a type of behaviour.
wrong.3: An official record is a document, not the act of misbehaving.

quiz.say: Which source is best for understanding the full scope of unreported theft?
quiz.why: Victim surveys directly ask people about experiences they might not report to the police.

wrong.0: This is too general; a specific source is needed for this problem.
wrong.2: Police records only count what is officially reported to them.
wrong.3: Court records only cover cases that have gone through the legal system.

quiz.say: If the police report 100 thefts, but the community survey suggests 150, what does this suggest?
quiz.why: The difference suggests that some crimes are happening but are not being officially recorded.

wrong.0: We should look for systemic gaps, not assume malicious intent.
wrong.1: The survey suggests the true rate might be higher than the official number.
wrong.3: The survey is valuable because it captures private experiences.
